Right ankle of a 25-year-old woman with painful posteromedial swelling. MRI c–f marks the accessory soleus belly and local course; coronal T1 panel f marks a muscular insertion on the medial calcaneus. Clinical photograph a and lateral radiograph b provide separate context and are not credited as MRI. Identified in this figure: Accessory soleus: labelled belly and limited visible course; Accessory soleus: local muscular distal insertion at the medial calcaneus. Identified in clinical photograph panels (a): Posteromedial right ankle swelling during plantar flexion. External photograph only; does not show the internal muscle course or an MRI signal. Identified in radiography panels (b): Obliterated Kager fat pad in a lateral right ankle radiograph. Projection context only; does not establish the muscle or tendon signal on MRI. Published sections do not establish the complete proximal attachment, full distal footprint, physical tissue dimensions, dynamic compression or a 3D volume. The source cases are symptomatic, not normal-reference examinations. Native repository JPEGs are small; a higher-resolution publisher master and individual DICOM acquisition metadata remain unverified. © 2020 Mihovil Plečko, Igor Knežević, Damjan Dimnjaković, Mario Josipović and Ivan Bojanić. Accessory Soleus Muscle: Two Case Reports with a Completely Different Presentation Caused by the Same Entity. Case Reports in Orthopedics 2020:8851920, DOI 10.1155/2020/8851920. CC BY 4.0. Right ankle of a 31-year-old woman with pain and plantar paresthesia; the case report documents concomitant tarsal tunnel syndrome. MRI b–f marks the accessory soleus and its tendinous distal insertion. Radiograph a is separate projection context. The source calls f axial, but its displayed anatomy appears longitudinal; that panel’s exact plane remains unresolved. Identified in this figure: Accessory soleus: labelled belly and limited visible course; Accessory soleus: local tendinous distal insertion at the medial calcaneus. Identified in radiography panels (a): Lateral right ankle projection with Kager fat-pad obliteration and calcaneal insula compacta. Radiography only; not credited as MRI or as proof of nerve compression. Published sections do not establish the complete proximal attachment, full distal footprint, physical tissue dimensions, dynamic compression or a 3D volume. The source cases are symptomatic, not normal-reference examinations. Native repository JPEGs are small; a higher-resolution publisher master and individual DICOM acquisition metadata remain unverified. Figure 3f has an unresolved source-caption/visual-plane discrepancy. © 2020 Mihovil Plečko, Igor Knežević, Damjan Dimnjaković, Mario Josipović and Ivan Bojanić.
